Subject: Quick question on what you consider "logs" / default retention

Hi Dylan,

We're completing a vendor assessment for our security & privacy team and need a clear view of Redwood's default retention behavior. Could you confirm the hosted defaults for the following items (VeloxHealth is considering the hosted API in the EU region):

- raw requests (user prompts / uploaded text)
- model outputs (final completions and chat responses)
- streamed fragments / partial token buffers (what persists if a stream is interrupted)
- transient caches (KV cache / session buffers used for streaming)
- derivative artifacts (embeddings, vector indexes)

Two additional asks: where are the records stored by default for EU customers (region/residency) and what is the standard erasure path if we request deletion?

We'd appreciate a short bulleted summary and any reference doc you can attach.

Thanks,
Simon

Subject: RE: Quick question on what you consider "logs" / default retention

Hi Simon — thanks for the clear list. Summary below; attaching a short matrix and an EU residency flowchart for your compliance team.

TL;DR (hosted API, default settings):
- raw requests (user prompts / uploads): retained for 30 days by default to support troubleshooting and quality monitoring. Customers can enable a strict "no-retain" flag at account level to avoid storage of user content.
- model outputs (final completions & chat messages): retained 30 days by default; included in the same troubleshooting snapshot as requests.
- streamed fragments / partial tokens: buffered to support streaming but only persisted in a short-lived buffer; default flush/evict window is 48 hours. Interrupted streams are not elevated to long-term storage unless they are part of a flagged support case.
- transient caches (KV/session buffers): treated as ephemeral runtime state; caches are stored on regional nodes and automatically evicted according to workload—default TTL is 48 hours.
- derivative artifacts (embeddings, indexes): not stored by default. If a customer requests embeddings to be persisted (for embeddings-as-a-service or index-building), those are written to a customer-owned blob (or Redwood-managed store if requested) and covered by the customer retention setting.

Residency & erasure:
- EU-hosted customers: by default, hosted data (requests, outputs, short-lived buffers) stays in the EU region. We route traffic and store logs in EU data centers for accounts provisioned in EU; control plane metadata for billing/ops may remain in our control plane (default in US) unless the account purchases our EU control-plane option.
- Deletion path: when you request a full erasure, we run an account-level purge which removes stored requests/outputs and derivative artifacts from active stores and schedules tombstone purge on backups according to our backup retention window. We return a Proof-of-Deletion summary (timestamped) once the active purges complete; full backup purge may take longer depending on the backup SLA.

Options for stricter models:
- No-retain flag (account-level): prevents retention of raw requests and outputs. Recommended for high-sensitivity workloads.
- Shortened retention: we can set a custom retention window (e.g., 7 days) for hosted accounts under an MSA/enterprise arrangement.
- Private deployment (VPC / on-prem): retention & residency are entirely under customer control — Redwood's default routines do not apply.

I'll attach the quickref matrix. If helpful, Karthik can add a one-page summary about how streaming vs finalization interacts with prefix caching (Karthik: see question about partial buffers below).

Cheers,
Dylan Brooks
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Adding a couple of technical clarifications on streaming and caching:

- Prefix/KV cache: the runtime maintains per-session KV like attention caches to serve low-latency streaming. Those caches are not persisted to long-term object stores by default—only in-memory/ephemeral regional storage and are subject to the 48-hour eviction window I mentioned.
- Interrupted streams: if a client reconnects and supplies a session token, we replay ephemeral state from the regional node for continuity; we do not materialize the full stream to object storage unless explicitly requested (support snapshot or customer debugging opt-in).
- Debug snapshots: during troubleshooting we capture a named snapshot (requests + outputs + minimal runtime traces) and store it for the lifecycle required to debug the issue. Snapshots are created only with an internal ticket or a customer opt-in.

Happy to jump on a 20-minute call to walk this through with your compliance team.

-Karthik
Principal Engineer, Runtime
